topic.title: We pick credit cards for the airport
topic.claim: Most of us chose our credit card for the lounge, not the money, and the bank knew we would.
topic.moment: Tapping the card at the lounge desk and feeling, for a second, like you made it.

turn.believed: People choose cards for the best rewards.
turn.actually: We choose the perk other people can see us use, and miss the points quietly losing value.

topic.because: A visible perk sells the card. Once you're in, the bank can trim the points and you rarely leave.
topic.payoff: Add up what your card actually gave you last year in rupees. Then compare it to the fee.
topic.behaviour: Users sign up for cards with lounge access, then barely track rewards or devaluations.
topic.mechanism: Status perks get people in; inertia keeps them in after the rewards shrink.
topic.group: Salaried card users who fly a few times a year
topic.send_to: The friend who checks lounge access before they check the flight time.
topic.why_now: Banks keep tightening lounge rules and reward rates, and people only notice at the airport.

score.why: We pay for what others can see; the lounge card is a perfect example and the bank knows it.

cover.headline: You picked your credit card for the [lounge], not the money
cover.sub: The perk people see you use is rarely the one that pays.

paragraphs: You picked your credit card for the lounge, not the money.
slides.why_swipe: Wait, didn't I pick it for the rewards?

paragraphs: Remember your first trip after the card arrived? You hand it over at the lounge desk, and there's a half second before the machine beeps.
Then it goes green. Filter coffee, a soft chair by the glass, the gate announcements a little muffled.
For a second, you feel like you made it.
slides.why_swipe: So what actually made you say yes to that card?

paragraphs: Go back to the sales call. They went through points on every swipe, extra on dining, a voucher at some milestone. You half listened.
Then they said "complimentary lounge access" and you said yes.
You opened the points page once in the first month. After that you only checked the total due.
slides.why_swipe: What were those points worth when you finally looked again?

paragraphs: A year later you open it to redeem. A steel bottle. A speaker you'd never buy. A voucher that gets you less than you remember.
**The points shrank while you weren't looking, and the bank counted on that.**
The lounge is what you can see, so the lounge sells the card. The points are what you can't see, so that's where the bank trims, with an email you archive.
slides.why_swipe: So why is the card still in your wallet?

paragraphs: Fair enough, if you fly every month, the lounge can pay for itself. You fly a few times a year.
The renewal fee SMS arrives. Switching means forms, a call, and a vague worry about your credit score. You let it go through.
So the lounge got you to sign, and the hassle keeps you there.
slides.why_swipe: How do you tell if your card was worth it?

paragraphs: Open last year's statements. Add the cashback and points you actually used, in rupees. Add a coffee and sandwich for each lounge visit you really made.
Put that one number next to the annual fee.
**If the fee wins, that filter coffee by the glass was the most expensive cup you drank all year.**

end.save: Come back to this when your card's renewal fee SMS arrives.
end.send: The friend who checks lounge access before they check the flight time.
end.promise: How money and status really move.

draft.caption: What's the most useless thing you've ever redeemed your card points for?
draft.alt_text: A six-slide carousel arguing that people choose credit cards for visible airport lounge access rather than rewards. It follows the reader from the proud moment the lounge machine beeps green, back to the sales call where the points pitch went past them but 'complimentary lounge access' got a yes. They check the points page once, then a year later find the redemption catalogue buys less than expected. The post explains that the visible lounge sells the card while the invisible points are where the bank trims value. Renewing happens out of habit because switching feels like a hassle. It ends with a test: add up the rupees the card actually gave back plus the lounge visits really made, and compare that with the annual fee. If the fee is bigger, the lounge coffee was the most expensive cup of the year.
